title: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild Review: Freedom Redefined
description: Nintendo’s open-air Zelda reinvention remains a landmark adventure built around curiosity, experimentation, and the freedom to make Hyrule your own.
body:
The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild does not simply move Zelda into an open world. It rebuilds the series around the idea that curiosity should be enough to pull the player forward.

From the moment Link steps out onto the Great Plateau, Hyrule feels less like a sequence of destinations and more like a place waiting to be understood. Mountains can be climbed, distant ruins can be investigated, weather changes the route ahead, and small environmental details constantly suggest that there may be something worth finding just beyond the next ridge.

That freedom was radical for Zelda in 2017, and it remains the game’s defining strength. Breath of the Wild trusts the player to choose a direction, experiment with its systems, fail without embarrassment, and build a personal journey out of dozens of small discoveries. Even years later, few open worlds make exploration feel this natural.
author: Rouane Mounssif
tags: The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild

cons: Limited build variety gives repeat playthroughs less mechanical freshness
Equipment durability can make valuable rewards feel temporary
Shrines become visually and structurally repetitive over a long playthrough
pros: One of the most naturally explorable open worlds ever designed
Exceptional freedom and systemic problem solving
Beautiful art direction and a powerful sense of atmosphere
Discovery feels personal instead of checklist-driven
A bold reinvention that still feels unmistakably like Zelda
reviewMeta.verdict: A landmark open-world adventure whose freedom, atmosphere, and sense of discovery remain extraordinary, even if equipment durability, repetitive shrine structure, and limited build variety reduce its long-term replay appeal.
reviewMeta.reviewCopy: Retrospective review. No promotional review copy was provided.

contentBlocks.text:
Breath of the Wild’s greatest achievement is how rarely it tells the player that there is only one correct way forward. Once the opening hours establish the basic rules, Hyrule becomes a web of possibilities rather than a chain of objectives.

A tower on the horizon, an unusual rock formation, smoke rising from a distant camp, or a mountain that looks barely reachable can become a self-created objective. The game constantly rewards that instinct. Sometimes the reward is tangible, but just as often it is a new view, an environmental puzzle, a character encounter, or the satisfaction of reaching somewhere that initially looked impossible.

That distinction matters. Many open-world games are enormous because they contain enormous lists. Breath of the Wild feels enormous because the player is allowed to decide what matters. Its map supports exploration rather than replacing it.
contentBlocks.heading: Freedom Is the Real Main Character

contentBlocks.text:
The world itself is designed around observation. Height matters because climbing creates new routes. Temperature matters because the environment can become an obstacle. Weather can interrupt a plan. Physics can turn an ordinary object into part of a solution.

These systems overlap in ways that make Hyrule feel unusually coherent. The game does not need a unique scripted interaction for every situation because its underlying rules are flexible enough to create unexpected outcomes on their own. A puzzle that seems to ask for one solution may accept several. A dangerous area can often be approached from a direction the designers never explicitly point toward.

This is where Breath of the Wild earns much of its reputation. Its freedom is not merely geographical. The player is given room to think, improvise, and occasionally discover a solution that feels almost accidental. That feeling of ownership makes even small victories memorable.
contentBlocks.heading: Hyrule Makes Curiosity Feel Useful

contentBlocks.text:
Breath of the Wild gives Link a compact set of core tools early and then spends the rest of the game finding new contexts for them. Instead of repeatedly handing out progression items that unlock one predetermined type of obstacle, Nintendo builds puzzles around systems that can interact with the world in multiple ways.

The result is a game that encourages experimentation. Objects have weight and momentum. Metal reacts differently from wood. Heat, electricity, wind, water, and gravity can become part of a solution. Even when the intended answer is obvious, the possibility of finding another route keeps the player engaged with the rules of the world rather than simply following instructions.

That systemic design also gives combat and traversal a playful quality. Breath of the Wild is often at its best when a plan goes wrong and the player has to improvise. Failure becomes part of discovery instead of something that simply sends you back to the last checkpoint.
contentBlocks.heading: The Physics Sandbox Keeps Zelda Playful

contentBlocks.text:
The shrine system is one of Breath of the Wild’s smartest structural ideas and one of its clearest limitations. Scattering compact puzzle spaces across Hyrule gives exploration a reliable rhythm: spot something unusual, investigate it, solve a challenge, and leave with meaningful progression.

Many individual shrines are excellent. Some contain elegant logic puzzles, clever physics interactions, or challenges that force the player to reconsider a familiar mechanic. The problem is accumulation. Their shared visual language and compact format begin to feel familiar long before the adventure is over.

The Divine Beasts provide larger puzzle spaces, but they do not fully replace the identity and variety of classic Zelda dungeons. Players who loved the older games for their themed temples, unique atmospheres, and long-form puzzle escalation may miss that sense of place. Breath of the Wild gains enormous freedom by breaking the traditional structure, but it gives up some of the handcrafted dungeon personality that once defined the series.
contentBlocks.heading: Shrines Are Clever, but Their Structure Eventually Repeats

contentBlocks.text:
The durability system is one of the game’s most debated choices because its purpose is easy to understand even when its consequences are frustrating. Breakable equipment prevents the player from finding one powerful option and ignoring the rest of the game’s loot. It encourages adaptation and keeps exploration relevant because replacements are always useful.

In the early game, that creates real tension. Improvised gear fits the survival tone, and constantly changing what Link carries can make encounters feel unpredictable. Over time, however, the same system can make rewards feel strangely temporary. Finding something exciting is immediately followed by the knowledge that it will eventually disappear through normal use.

That trade-off becomes more noticeable late in the adventure, when inventory management has stopped feeling novel and the player has already seen most of the available combat styles. The mechanic succeeds at forcing variety in the moment, but it does not create the deeper build variety that would make a second full playthrough feel substantially different.
contentBlocks.heading: Equipment Durability Encourages Adaptation, but Weakens Attachment

contentBlocks.text:
Breath of the Wild’s visual direction has aged remarkably well because it prioritizes shape, color, movement, and atmosphere over raw detail. Hyrule can look peaceful, lonely, inviting, or dangerous without needing constant cinematic spectacle.

The restrained soundtrack is equally important. Music often steps back while wind, wildlife, footsteps, weather, and distant environmental sounds define the journey. When stronger musical themes do appear, they carry more weight because the game has allowed silence and ambience to become part of its identity.

The story follows the same philosophy. Much of Hyrule’s history is reconstructed through ruins, memories, and scattered conversations. The main plot is relatively simple, but the melancholy of a kingdom already lost gives exploration emotional context. You are not discovering a world waiting to be saved from destruction; you are wandering through the remains of a disaster and slowly understanding what happened.
contentBlocks.heading: Its Quiet Presentation Gives Hyrule a Lasting Identity

contentBlocks.text:
Breath of the Wild offers an enormous amount to complete, but quantity is not the same as replayability. Its most powerful currency is surprise. The first time you discover a hidden village, solve an environmental mystery, reach a distant landmark, or realize that one of the world’s systems can be manipulated in an unexpected way, the experience feels personal.

A second playthrough cannot fully recreate that discovery. Link also has less room for fundamentally different character builds than players might expect from such an open-ended game. You can favor different approaches in individual encounters, but progression does not support radically distinct character identities in the way a role-playing game might.

That does not diminish the original journey. If anything, it highlights what Breath of the Wild does best. This is a game built around the feeling of not knowing what lies ahead. Once that mystery is gone, Hyrule remains beautifully designed, but some of its magic naturally becomes harder to reproduce.
contentBlocks.heading: The First Journey Is More Powerful Than the Second

conclusion:
==Breath of the Wild remains one of Nintendo’s most important games because its freedom is supported by design rather than scale alone. Hyrule rewards curiosity, its systems encourage experimentation, and the game repeatedly creates the feeling that a discovery belongs to the player rather than to a checklist.==

==Its weaknesses are real. Breakable equipment can make rewards feel temporary, the repeated shrine aesthetic eventually wears thin, and limited build variety means the game’s sense of discovery is much harder to reproduce on a full replay. But those flaws sit inside an adventure whose first journey is extraordinary. Breath of the Wild did not simply modernize Zelda; it changed what players expected from open-world exploration.==

==9.6/10 — OUTSTANDING==
conclusionHeading: A Landmark Adventure That Still Feels Free
